title: Where would they go?
hookLine: the urge to quit, loud as a person in the room; Shantideva searches for where it lives and finds no address
tomorrow: so many rules to keep. is there one guard that keeps them all?

lines: THE URGE TO QUIT, IN THE ROOM.
TURN AND LOOK STRAIGHT AT IT.
cards: Some nights the urge to quit is so loud it feels like a person in the room. Quit the class. Quit the team.
Close the laptop on the application and never open it again. It has a voice, a deadline, a whole argument ready. And here's the odd thing about yesterday's question.
When you actually turn and look straight at that urge, really look, it gets strangely hard to find. Shantideva tried this. He went looking for the address of his enemies.

teach.b: Here's the search, close to how he lays it out at the end of chapter four. An ordinary enemy, driven out of a country, goes somewhere else, regroups, and comes back stronger. But the afflictions?

teach.h: SEEN THROUGH, WHERE WOULD THEY GO?
teach.b: Once seen through with the eye of wisdom, he asks, where would they go? Where would they stay, to gather strength and return? So he checks.

teach.h: NOT IN THE THING, NOT IN THE EYES.
teach.b: Is anger in the thing that set it off? No; the same thing doesn't anger everyone. Is it in the eyes, the ears, the senses?
Not there either. Somewhere in between? Somewhere else?
He can't find a home for it anywhere.
And he concludes that the afflictions are like an illusion: real enough to push you around, and nowhere to be found when you look. This is a practice, not just an argument.

The urge to quit, looked at closely, turns out to be a tightness in the chest, a sentence on repeat, a picture of failing. Each piece is small, and none of them is a front door. You don't have to defeat it.
You just ask it, kindly and honestly, where it lives.

how: In Mahayana practice, investigating where an emotion lives, in the object, the senses or the mind, is a common meditation; teachers often use it to loosen an urge's grip rather than to suppress it.

games.q: what does “where would they go?” mean?
o: an urge, looked at closely, has no home to retreat to
a lost thought that wanders off and comes back later
a feeling you hide away so nobody else can see it

games.q: the search for an address — tap the pairs.
p: the thing that set it off
real enough to push, nowhere when sought

s: Shantideva says an urge is unreal, so it can't push you around
like an illusion, it's real enough to push you, and nowhere to be found when you look.
he looks for anger in the object, the senses, in between and elsewhere
and can't find a home for it anywhere.

games.q: a friend is sure she should drop out of the school play two days before opening night. she can't say why, just 'i have to.' what do you ask her?
o: 'where is the i-have-to, exactly? in your stomach? in a thought? let's look.'
'then quit. if the feeling is that strong, it must be telling you something true.'
'just ignore it. feelings like that don't mean anything at all.'
games.why: Shantideva doesn't obey the affliction or wave it off. he looks for where it lives, and finds no home for it.

practice: Close your eyes and call up one urge you've had today, even a small one. Look for it in the body: is it in the chest, the jaw, the hands? Look for it in the words running through your head.
Wherever you find a piece, rest your attention there and ask, quietly, is this where you live?

wordCard.voice: Where would they go: Shantideva's question for the afflictions once they're seen through. They have no home to retreat to.

orig.note: Sanskrit: wisdom, insight; the 'eye of wisdom' that sees through the afflictions. Pali panna.

carryVoice: Pocket this question for the next loud urge: where would it live? That's the end of chapter four.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 4.45-4.47 (an ordinary enemy expelled regroups; the afflictions, abandoned by the eye of wisdom, where would they go? not in objects, not in the senses, not in between, nor elsewhere; like an illusion)
